---
title: "Data-driven archetypes of farmland change"
author: Carolyn Koehn
abstract: |
  Approximately 1.5 million km$^2$ of land globally was converted from agriculture to highly developed areas between 1992 and 2018. The processes leading to this conversion are variable, but most farmland protection policy focuses on controlling urban sprawl. A better understanding of the multiple contexts in which farmland loss occurs can inform diverse and targeted policies for agricultural land protection. To identify multiple contexts of agricultural change, we used a mixed methods archetypes approach that identifies recurring patterns of variables in social-ecological systems across different spaces and time periods. We combined finite Gaussian mixture model cluster analysis and qualitative data to find recurring patterns of change over time in 26 counties in southern Idaho's Snake River Plain, a region of the western United States [US] with both high agricultural production and high population growth where agricultural lands are at risk of conversion. We used data linked to resource and actor variables in a commonly used social-ecological systems framework. Specifically, we calculated descriptive metrics for 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020 from the US Census, land use/land cover spatial data, the US Census of Agriculture, and other public data sources. We found that these 26 counties over 4 time points clustered into 5 resource clusters and 5 actors clusters. Resource clusters were strongly driven by developed, crop-, and federal lands, housing density, and land near major roadways, whereas actor clusters were strongly driven by degree of geographical isolation and population density. We then selected three counties from the full pool of counties to do qualitative analysis of interview data and link those insights with the results of the quantitatively derived clusters. Through combined quantitative and qualitative approaches, we found that agricultural land loss occurs in multiple contexts, including along the rural-urban continuum and in more rural areas with recreation access. We reveal spatially distant counties in the same archetype that may be able to share successful farmland protection policies, as well as neighboring counties in different archetypes that will likely require different policy pathways to protect farmland. We intentionally used publicly available data so that this approach could be applied to many areas grappling with agricultural land loss.
date: last-modified

# Introduction

Approximately 1.5 million km$^2$ of land globally has been converted from agriculture to urban and highly developed areas between 1992 and 2018, amounting to 7.5% of total global land cover change in that 25-year period [@radwan2021]. The pathway to conversion is often attributed to urban or suburban sprawl [@chen2020; @vanvliet2017], and land use projections for future agricultural land loss are based on the assumption that population growth will drive urban development of agricultural lands based on their proximity to an urban center [i.e. land rent/"growth machine" theory, @meyfroidt2018; @xie2023; @chen2020; @haney2015]. Other pathways to agricultural land conversion, such as housing development in rural settlements and increased local commodity processing [@ju2018; @jiang2019], are described by less spatially-explicit theories [e.g. rural gentrification, @gosnell2011; "technology treadmill," @meyfroidt2018] and so are not operationalized in spatial land use prediction models. The focus on urban sprawl in farmland loss predictions leads to a mismatch between the identification of threatened farmlands, policy implemented to protect farmland, and actual farmland conversion. For example, urban growth boundaries are effective in containing development in some small cities but ineffective in others [@dempsey2013]. In order to enact effective policies to protect high quality agricultural lands, it is critical to understand the multiple pathways by which those lands are converted to other uses and where they are occurring. There are three recurring patterns of farmland loss that have been described separately in a number of case studies: urban/suburban sprawl, amenity migration, and agricultural industrialization.
<!-- Even when other pathways to agricultural land loss impact a smaller land area compared to urban sprawl, they can have significant negative impacts on local ecology and crop production [@zhu2022] and social and community well-being [@smith2001]. -->

Urban sprawl is a widely recognized cause of agricultural land loss. As the population in urban centers grows, there is increased need for housing. While cities may create denser housing in the urban center to accommodate a larger population, they often expand outwards, creating spacious suburban neighborhoods [@dieleman2004]. As suburbs encroach on agricultural land, farmland fragmentation makes farming more difficult and encourages further development [@latruffe2014; @qiu2015; @freedgood2020]. Rising land values near urban areas are a critical barrier to entry for young farmers, which is particularly problematic in the context of a nationwide aging farming population looking to retire [@kuethe2014; @sheridan2007]. Farmland fragmentation and rising land values create a higher likelihood that near-urban farmlands will be sold for development rather than continuing in agriculture. High quality croplands are especially susceptible to urban sprawl as both farming and housing development are easiest on flat lands with more access to freshwater [@halperin2023; @bren2017]. Demographically, urbanized areas have higher population density and diversified employment opportunities compared to more rural areas, and suburban areas in particular are linked to higher education quality and lower levels of poverty [@dumont2023; @burdick2017]. There are a number of adaptations that farmers in urbanizing areas have deployed to prevent farmland loss with varying success, including building social capital with non-farmers, diversifying operations, succession planning, and utilizing policy instruments like agricultural easements and zoning [@sharp2003; @inwood2012; @bengston2004]. Urban and suburban sprawl are a prominent force in agricultural land loss and are accounted for in many land use change models focused on agricultural lands [@xie2023; @chen2020; @haney2015].

Industrial development is another driver of agricultural land loss, but agricultural change in the industrial context manifests differently than in urban sprawl. Across Asia, conversion of agricultural land to industry use precedes urban sprawl or occurs alongside urban sprawl [@azadi2011; @tuyen2013; @zhou2020]. In Europe, a large portion of manufacturing was shifted to rural areas in the late 1970s [@keeble1983], and food manufacturing is an important component of many rural economies [@rizov2011]. In the United States, food manufacturing occurs in both urban and rural areas, especially those with access to raw materials (e.g. milk), labor availability, and sufficient infrastructure, including interstates, water, and electricity [@lambert2009; @compton2018]. Additionally, the presence of one manufacturing facility is correlated with the presence of other facilities, as well as with associated commodity production [@lambert2009]. Besides conversion of agricultural land for manufacturing facilities, these factories can attract non-local workers who need housing, yet their settlement patterns may be different from those of urban sprawl populations. Farmworkers producing raw commodities may be housed on farms, provided housing by their employers in nearby towns or cities, or find their own housing, and rapid Hispanic population growth is associated with food processing plants [@garni2018; @quandt2015; @lichter2012]. Farmers near food processing plants can increase their sales by increasing their production of the raw materials used by the nearby industry, but this comes at considerable input and labor costs [@jafri2024]. Thus, industrial development involves different demands for land and farmer adaptations compared to other drivers of farmland loss.

Amenity migration, the migration of urban dwellers to rural areas for specific lifestyle amenities, is a pathway to rural land change including agricultural land loss [@abrams2012]. Rural sprawl associated with amenity migration tends to be less dense than urban sprawl, resulting in larger areas of land affected, but with less intensity [@radeloff2005]. Amenity migrants with agricultural estates do not rely on agricultural production as a means of income; though they may engage in some form of farming (including hobby farms) or lease lands to local producers, they may also use their lands exclusively for non-production uses like recreation and conservation [@abrams2012; @abrams2013; @matarrita2025]. Local jobs are primarily low-wage service jobs, and this combined with rising property values can push low income households farther out of the high-amenity community [@sherman2018; @loeffler2007; @abrams2012]. Thus, agricultural producers may face rising land costs and falling off-farm wages, the need to lease land, and the fragmentation of agricultural lands by migrant estates and commuter roads, but they also may find receptive collaborators in amenity migrants who want to keep lands in agriculture [@matarrita2025; @abrams2013]. Amenity migration is a distinct pathway to agricultural land loss that differs in cause and effects from urban sprawl and industrial expansion, and requires different policy and planning approaches to address.

Since agricultural land conversion occurs via different processes in different contexts, farmland loss may be well described by archetype analysis. Archetypes are recurring patterns of social-ecological variables that build towards middle-range theories -- generalizations that describe causal pathways within a well-bounded range of phenomena [@meyfroidt2018; @oberlack2019]. The three farmland loss pathways described above, urban/suburban sprawl, agricultural industrialization, and amenity migration, are distinct phenomena that require context-specific policies to manage farmland conversion. Yet the spatial distribution of these phenomena, including potential overlaps, and their progression through time have not been analyzed in a formal archetype analysis. In the United States, long-term public datasets enable longitudinal studies of land use and demographic change that can construct dynamic archetypes, patterns of social-ecological variables that re-occur across both space and time. The intentional use of public data ensures that this analysis can be implemented across the country.

The Snake River Plain of Idaho is an ideal place to study multiple processes of farmland loss because it is experiencing different drivers of agricultural land conversion across its counties. We hypothesize that land use change is occurring due to urban/suburban sprawl, amenity migration, and agricultural industrialization in different areas across the region. This research will aid in identifying where distinct processes of land use change are occurring, contributing to a diverse toolbox for agricultural lands protection in diverse localities. We calculated descriptive metrics for 26 Idaho counties in 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020 (104 units total) from the US Census, land use/land cover spatial data, and the US Census of Agriculture. Our research questions were:

1. Are there identifiable archetypes of social-ecological subsystems (resource and actors) in Idaho's Snake River Plain, and which demographic, economic, and remotely sensed indicators are the most important characteristics of those archetypes?
2. What is the relationship between these archetypes and farmland loss, and do the archetypes identify cases of urban sprawl, amenity migration, and industrialization?
3. Are there counties that have shifted archetypes through time, and what are their characteristics?
4. In what ways do actors describe drivers of community change within archetype shifts indicating urban sprawl, amenity migration, or industrialization?

# Methods

## Study Area

The Snake River Plain ecoregion of the United States [@ecoregions] intersects with 26 Idaho counties (109,700 km$^2$). It contains  productive croplands [@freedgood2020], localized yet rapidly growing highly developed urban areas [@census_metro], and public rangelands grazed by livestock (@freedgood2020). This region features two primary ecological zones, the river plain and the shrub steppe, and a diverse range of social systems, from urban and exurban systems to dryland agriculture and rural public lands, that together form a diverse array of social-ecological systems [@aho2022]. 

Farmland protection in southern Idaho is based on the 1981 Right to Farm section of Idaho Code, which protects farmlands from nuisance lawsuits [@IDRightToFarm], and the 1975 Local Land Use Planning Act, which mandates that cities and counties must plan and zone [@IDLLUPA; @meyer2025]. Therefore, farmland protection actions and funding from 1990-2020 in southern Idaho occur at the county level or lower. Farmland protection is mainly accomplished through zoning that prevents development on farmland and perpetual easements established in partnership with local land trusts. Before 2020, Idaho's Snake River Plain contained 64 agricultural easements totaling to 271 $km^2$, or 0.2% of the total study area [@pald], a very small amount since establishing easements without state matching funds is costly.

## Data Selection

The social-ecological systems [SES] framework first published in 2007 by Elinor Ostrom is a conceptual framework that provides a list of variables that may affect the outcome of a SES [@ostrom2009; @partelow2018]. For comparative analysis of multiple case studies, the focus of archetype analysis, it provides structure and variables for comparison [@oberlack2016; @partelow2018]. The framework introduces variables describing four major subsystems in a SES: resource systems, resource units, governance systems, and actors, as well as variables describing the interactions of these systems, the related ecosystem, and the social, economic, and political setting [@ostrom2009]. Readily-available public data can describe some of these systems comprehensively, and while it is difficult to quantify indicators for others [@partelow2018]. We chose to focus on three subsystems that are easily described by quantitative public data: the resource system and resource units, which we combine into a single resource model, and the actors. We linked data available from 1990-2020 to second-tier variables in these subsystems of the SES framework based on expert knowledge from the authors. Some second-tier variables are excluded because no relevant data sources could be found, but it is common to analyze subsets of SES variables in the SES literature [@partelow2018]. We scaled all data by mean normalization [@hennig2016]. Detailed data sources and processing steps for each indicator and year can be found in Appendix A.

## Gaussian Mixed Model Clustering

We ran two separate cluster analyses, one with the resource variables and one with the actor variables, in order to characterize the resource and actor subsystems of the counties separately.

### Model Selection

There are three components to model selection in Gaussian-based cluster modeling: variable selection, number of clusters, and cluster shape. First, variable selection is used to remove redundant or irrelevant variables from the data that could degrade the performance of model-based clustering [@bouveyron2019]. Reducing the dimensions of a model reduces the number of parameters needed to specify the covariance matrix [@bouveyron2019]. Dimension reduction is important in this analysis because we have relatively few observations (n=104) compared to dimensions (30 resource variables, 18 actor variables), and we cannot estimate more model parameters than observations. We can test more combinations of cluster shape and number of clusters that require more parameters if we reduce the number of dimensions [@scrucca2023; @bouveyron2019]. While all of our chosen indicators convey important information about a social-ecological agricultural system, we decided to remove redundant indicators in order to test more clustering configurations.

We identified redundant indicators by systematically checking single variables for exclusion using a backward stepwise greedy search, which allowed us to take variable dependencies into account [@bouveyron2019]. We began with the full set of variables, then tested the exclusion of each indicator individually, dropping the single most redundant variable, as identified by BIC. Then, this step was repeated with the remaining indicators until all indicators were identified as useful for clustering. At all steps after the first, we tested the inclusion of all dropped variables and added any that showed new evidence for clustering importance after other variables were dropped. We used the R package `clustvarsel` for this variable selection process (v2.3.5, see @clustvarsel for a full description of the backward stepwise greedy search). 

The next two steps of model selection are selecting the shape of the clusters in dimensional space (e.g. spherical vs elliptical) and the number of clusters, both of which we implemented with R package `mclust` [v6.1.1, @scrucca2023]. We tested for a range of 1-5 clusters in each model, as it's recommended to vary the number of possible clusters between 1 and the next integer after $n^{0.3}$ [4 < 104$^{0.3}$ < 5, @biernacki2006]. We tested all 14 possible model shapes (see @scrucca2023 for a description of all possible shapes), though some model shapes, which require many parameters, could not be tested. For the resource model, we could not test shapes VEE, EVE, VVE, EVV, or VVV with >2 groups. For the actors model, we could not test shapes EVE or VVE with >3 groups.

Because clustering models are sensitive to their initialization, we ran each model 200 times with random initializations. We selected the best model structure of the 200 runs using BIC, and the log likelihoods for the 200 runs of both models indicated no evidence of alternative local solutions [@bauer2021].

### Selected Model Structures

After variable selection, we removed (1) agriculture support jobs, (2) shrubland change, (3) lake area, and (4) land in farms from the resource model. The optimal number of clusters was 5, and the optimal cluster shape was VEV [ellipsoidal, with variable volume, equal shape, and variable orientation in dimensional space, @scrucca2023].

After variable selection, we removed most indicators from the actors model, retaining (1) population density, (2) the first principal component of employment, (3) number of hired agricultural workers, and (4) the first two principal components for geographical isolation. The optimal number of clusters was 5, and the optimal cluster shape was EVV [ellipsoidal, with equal volume, variable shape, and variable orientation in dimensional space, @scrucca2023].

To determine the most influential variables in each model, we used dimension reduction to maximally separate clusters, which is similar to principle component analysis [@scrucca2023]. We multiplied the contribution of each indicator to each reduced dimension by the overall explanatory power of each dimension, then summed each variable's contributions. We used this value to identify the variables that were most important for creating the most separated clusters.

A data-driven methodological routine to identify key indicators for social-ecological system archetype mapping. Environmental Research Letters, 17(4), 045019. -->

# Results

## Cluster Descriptions

### Resource Clusters

The most influential variables in the resource model were: (1) developed land, (2) housing density, (3) non-federal land near major roadways, and (4) federal land (@suppfigb-R-influential).

```{r}
#| label: "label county data"

clust_dat <- list()

clust_dat[["Resource"]] <- read.csv("data/model results/clust_dat_resource.csv") %>%
  left_join(aoi, by = c("county" = "NAME")) %>%
  st_as_sf()

  left_join(aoi, by = c("county" = "NAME")) %>%
  st_as_sf()

resource_means <- clust_dat$Resource %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))

actor_means <- clust_dat$Actors %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE))
```

#### Cluster R1: Risk of urban sprawl -- Flat land with accessible urban amenities

Characteristic resources of R1 are crop- and developed land, high access to highways and urban areas, higher housing density, more healthcare workers, and flatter land (@fig-R-CIs, @supptblb-data-r1). This cluster has more small farms than any other. These counties have experienced higher cropland loss and developed land gain compared to other resource clusters (@suppfigb-R-ranges, @supptblb-data-r1). This cluster is home to Boise, the largest city in Idaho, and neighboring Canyon County, known for its high quality farmland but experiencing urban sprawl from the Boise metropolitan area.

#### Cluster R2: Risk of urban sprawl, amenity migration, and/or industrial agriculture -- Flat land near natural and urban amenities

R2 is closer to national parks and ski areas, and is closer to urban areas while not containing much urban or developed land. Its unique characteristics are less forest presence and higher shrubland cover, flatter land, and the higher presence of large farms and cropland. While farms in this cluster are still being lost, these counties are losing farms at a slower rate than other clusters and less farms operate at a loss (@fig-R-CIs). Farmland and cropland loss are average for the study area, and the rates of developed land gain is low. These counties tend to have lower home values than R2 (@supptblb-data-r3).

#### Cluster R3: Risk of amenity migration -- Access to mountain recreation and urban amenities

Characteristic resources of R3 are a greater presence of forestland and more steep lands (@fig-R-CIs). These counties are closer to ski areas and have a higher presence of recreation land, have an average presence of lakes and rivers, and support more jobs in hospitality (@suppfigb-R-ranges, @supptblb-data-r2). There is little developed or urban land, and both housing and farm density are low. However, most of the land in these counties lie within 50 miles of an urban area and its amenities, and access to major roadways is average for the study area (@supptblb-data-r2). These counties have higher home values compared to other clusters (@supptblb-data-r2), indicating the appeal of the natural amenities and non-urban nature of these counties. Rates of cropland loss and developed land gain are fairly low compared to other clusters.

#### Cluster R4: Risk of amenity migration and industrialized agriculture -- Rural agriculture as natural amenity

Cluster R4 has less presence of natural land covers like forest and shrublands, and average cover of cropland and developed land (@fig-R-CIs). Though there are many rivers, access to other natural amenities such as ski areas, national parks, lakes, forests, and recreation lands are low (@suppfigb-R-ranges). Like R2 and R3, there is not much urban land in these counties, but almost all of their lands are within 50 miles of an urban area (@supptblb-data-r5). Rates of cropland loss are low, while developed land gain and farm loss are average for the study area (@fig-R-CIs).

#### Cluster R5: Low risk of farmland loss -- Very isolated counties with few natural amenities

The unique characteristics of R5 are more shrubland cover, less cropland cover, a greater amount of federal land, greater distance from urban areas, and less access to highways (@fig-R-CIs). Natural amenities are also few, with less river miles, minimal lake area, average presence of recreation and forest land, and long distances to a ski areas (@suppfigb-R-ranges). Similar to R2, R5 has more large farms and less farms operating at a loss. The low cropland cover of R5 indicates that agriculture in these counties is more focused on livestock grazing (@supptblb-data-r4). R5 has low rates of cropland loss and developed land gain, and it is also losing fewer farms than other counties (@suppfigb-R-ranges).

### Actors Clusters

The most influential variables in the resource model were: (1) geographic isolation and (2) population density (@suppfigb-A-influential).

#### Cluster A1: Metropolitan counties with high population growth

The defining characteristics of A1 are its high population density, low employment in agriculture, and metropolitan workforce, with most people living and working in the same metropolitan county, or living in Canyon County and commuting to nearby Boise for work (@fig-A-CIs, @supptblb-data-a1). A1 also has high population growth, higher incomes, and a higher percentage of residents with a Bachelor's degree (@suppfigb-A-ranges). Despite a lower proportion of residents in agricultural production, the number of hired agricultural workers is fairly high for the study area, indicating the high production needs of the farms that remain in these counties (@fig-A-CIs). A1 also has the highest share of farms that are fully owned by the producer, as well as a higher percentage of farms operating at a loss. These farm labor, tenure, and profit rates indicate that farming in these counties is financially difficult, and renting land to expand farming operations is especially challenging.

#### Cluster A2: Small cities 

Cluster A2's unique characteristic is that all its counties are micropolitan (contain an urban area with 10,000-49,999 residents, @supptblb-data-a3), and most workers live and work in the same county. A2 is similar to A1 (high population growth with wealthier, highly educated residents), but experiences most indicators to a lesser degree. Population density and growth are high, but not as high as A1, and residents have higher incomes and more are college educated, but not at the levels of A1 (@suppfigb-A-ranges). Like A1, a lower percentage of residents are employed in agriculture, but there are a higher percentage in retail trade and lower percentage in construction compared to A1 (@supptblb-data-a3).

#### Cluster A3: Small town counties grow as quickly as small cities

Counties in A3 are "small town" counties (contain an urban area with population 5,000-9,999), have low population density, and are fairly geographically isolated with most workers living and working in the same county or another small town county (@fig-A-CIs, @supptblb-data-a4). In many ways, A3 is similar to A4, with similar employment in agriculture, lower incomes, and fewer people with a Bachelor's degree (@fig-A-CIs). Population growth rates are similar in A2, A3, and A4, and this population growth fuels transitions to more urbanized clusters.

#### Cluster A4: Rural counties with less agriculture

A4 and A5 are very similar in that they are rural counties, meaning they do not contain an urban area with more than 5,000 residents, with low population density, moderate population growth, and fewer residents with a Bachelor's degree (@fig-A-CIs, @supptblb-data-a2). A4 is differentiated by fewer workers in agriculture, more people commuting to more urban counties, and slightly higher incomes compared to the rural counties in A5 (@supptblb-data-a2, @suppfigb-A-ranges).

#### Cluster A5: Geographically isolated rural counties with less economic opportunity

Like A2, A5 has rural counties with low population density, moderate population growth, and less residents with a Bachelor's degree (@fig-A-CIs, @supptblb-data-a5). However, compared to A2, more residents of A5 counties are working in agriculture, and less commute to more urbanized areas (@supptblb-data-a5). A5 has lower incomes and hires fewer agricultural workers compared to other clusters (@suppfigb-A-ranges).

## Cluster Transitions {#sec-transitions}

There was one resource transition in the study period: Power County transitioned from R3 (Access to mountain recreation and urban amenities) to R2 (Flat land near natural and urban amenities) in 2000. This can be attributed to a lower percentage of residents employed in hospitality, as well as less large farms and less cropland loss after 2000.

Looking across actor transitions, we can put together a common progression through actor archetypes. The most rural and isolated archetype is A5 (geographically isolated rural counties with less economic opportunity). From A5, counties transition to A4 (rural counties with less agriculture), keeping their rural nature but transitioning away from traditional rural careers, or they transition to A3 (small town counties grow as quickly as small cities), if population growth is concentrated and creates an urban area. A4 may further transition to A3 if an urban area is created (i.e. Gem County, 1990 to 2000). Next, A3 counties transition to A2 (small cities) once enough population growth has occurred to reclassify the small towns in A3 counties to the micropolitan areas of A2 counties. Finally, A2 counties may become metropolitan A1 counties if enough population growth occurs, but in our study area, this only occurred adjacent to another A1 county.

# Discussion

## Archetype analysis links spatially and temporally separated but thematically similar counties

This analysis recontextualizes counties in the study area, allowing us to link counties that are spatially separated but have similar resources and actors. For example, Twin Falls County and Bingham County are both R2-A2 in 2020 -- small cities with flat land near natural and urban amenities. The archetype shift in Bingham County occurred between 2000-2010, indicating that they will face similar agricultural changes and risks of farmland conversion to Twin Falls, but at a delayed rate. Indeed, [connecting example]. Bingham County may be able to learn from farmland protection interventions in Twin Falls. Unfortunately, our qualitative data suggests that farmland protection has been extremely limited in Twin Falls. Instead of suggesting transferable policies, we propose that Bingham County should consider its possible "no policy implemented" future may look similar to Twin Falls, and decide if they would like to implement policies that guide their county's future in a different direction. Another example is Teton County and Minidoka County, which are both in actor archetype A4 -- rural counties with less agriculture. Though they are in different resource archetypes, they are both dealing with agricultural and community change stemming from population growth. One example of this is new Latter-Day Saints temples under construction or newly completed in counties neighboring both Teton and Minidoka [cite]. Our preliminary qualitative data revealed that producers and old newcomers are allied in advocating for farmland protection in Teton County. It is unclear if this alliance arises from Teton's combination of actors and resources, or if it is possible in multiple resource archetypes. If the producer-old newcomer alliance primarily arises from actor type alone, Minidoka County might pursue a similar alliance of farmland protection advocates.

Archetype analysis also revealed gaps in our knowledge that can be used for future studies of community change. In the beginning of this study, we hypothesized that we would identify archetypes related to three major phenomena that lead to farmland conversion -- urban sprawl, agricultural industrialization, and amenity migration -- and we conducted interviews and qualitative analysis in a selection of counties where these processes were occurring. However, the archetype analysis also revealed the R4 (rural agriculture as natural amenity) group of counties that we had not identified as requiring targeted qualitative data collection. Local knowledge suggests that farmland conversion may be in its beginning stages, as farmers in these counties are receiving cold calls about selling their land to prospective buyers (David Anderson, personal communication). This arcehtype will require further study to understand its unique dynamics of agricultural change.

Dynamic archetype analysis (archetype change through time) is an especially useful tool for considering multifaceted, temporal SES dynamics. Dynamic archetypes are a fairly recent innovation with the archetype analysis literature, and have primarily been used to study how a major change or "shock" to a system results in archetype change. For example, @orozco2024 used dynamic archetypes to study the effect of EU agricultural policies on agricultural changes in Germany. Our study is located in a place and time where farmland protection policy is fairly weak and has not changed. Absent major policy change, we were able to build a proposed timeline of actor archetype transitions that we expect to occur by observing all the transitions that took place in our study period (see @sec-transitions). We propose that this timeline reveals likely future scenarios that each county may face, which can inform proactive policy design. Longitudinally comparable datasets are important for this work. In this analysis, we've laid the blueprint to use public data in this way for any region in the US.

## Multiple resource archetypes are at risk of farmland loss, actor archetypes indicate likely rate of development

R1, the cluster losing the most cropland and land in farms and gaining the most developed land, contains both counties that exhibit the traditional patterns of urban sprawl -- Ada and Canyon Counties, which contain Idaho's largest city (Boise) and its metropolitan area. However, other archetypes (R2-R4) are also gaining developed land. These outcomes are tied not only to the resource archetype, but also the actor archetype. In both R2 and R3, the largest gains in developed land are observed when the actor archetype is small cities (A2) or rural with less agriculture (A4). This indicates that in these resource contexts, certain actor archetypes are more likely to fuel non-farm development: the growing small city and the rural area transitioning away from an agricultural economy.

Three resource archetypes at risk of farmland loss are either on flat lands with access to urban amenities (R1, R2) or near mountain recreation (R3). These results align with existing research on farmland conversion. Flat, accessible lands, such as those in R1 and R2, are prime sites for residential and commercial development as well as farming [@halperin2023], and in these resource archetypes, residential development is proceeding while cropland area declines. On the other end of the spectrum, rural areas near mountain recreation offer many natural amenities, and non-farm residential and commercial development caters to a growing population of amenity migrants [@abrams2012]. R4, rural agriculture as natural amenity, also has access to urban amenities (all those lands are within 50 miles of an urban area) and is experiencing various levels of development. This is a newer type of amenity migration that is attracting less affluent amenity migrants [@matarrita2025].

Our finding that some actor archetypes have higher rates of development than others, particularly that growing small town counties have lower rates of development than some rural counties in R2 and R3, was more surprising. This finding highlights both the strengths and limitations of the USDA Rural-Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes, which we adapted for this analysis and were strong drivers of the actor archetypes. The strength of the RUCA methodology is that the urban population threshold used to distinguish between small town and micropolitan counties is useful for delineating different rates of development in R2 and R3 counties. However, our clustering identified two distinct rural actor archetypes, one of which had higher rates of development (A4) than the other (A5), that are not reflected in the "rural"  RUCA category.


## Qualitative data enriches quantitative archetypes

Qualitative data enhances archetype analysis by providing further context and validation of our findings. A limitation of the data driven archetypes is their failure to detect changes in counties without archetype shifts. Our actor archetypes were designed to reflect community change, but they are strongly tied to data on metropolitan, micropolitan, small town, and rural areas, determined by population and housing density thresholds [@ruca]. When a county remains between these thresholds, changes in its actors are not as easily detected. This occurred in Twin Falls County, where interview data revealed dramatic changes to the community that were not captured by the quantitative archetypes, while at the same time affirming its unchanged economic reliance on agricultural products. The qualitative data underscore the need to consider change even in places that have not changed archetypes through time.

In the rapidly expanding field of archetype analysis for sustainability science, there has been a need to establish methods for archetype validation. Robust archetypes require both internal validation to demonstrate that cases in each archetype are indeed more similar to each other than to other cases and external validation to demonstrate the extent to which the archetypes are applicable outside the study [@eisenack2019]. We contend that qualitative data collection is a method for both types of validation. In this study, we used qualitative data for limited internal validation. In this preliminary analysis of the qualitative data, we were only able to analyze data for one case each in 3 of the 5 resource and actor archetypes. These data build a fuller picture of community change in these archetypes than could be constructed with quantitative data alone. Future research may be able to use qualitative data collection in multiple cases in each archetype to reveal nuanced similarities and differences in outcomes and social-ecological attributes between cases, furthering the use of qualitative data for internal archetype validation. Qualitative data can also be used for external validation when a rich literature of case studies exists for similar phenomena outside the study area. For example, amenity migration in the western United States is a well studied phenomenon in rural sociology. Based on numerous case studies, we believe the R3 archetype is valid in areas near mountains across the western United States [@sherman2018; @abrams2013]. Linking quantitative data, qualitative data, and published case studies of amenity migration in future research could validate the total extent of the "access to mountain recreation and urban amenities" (R3) archetype.

## Limitations

A longstanding difficulty with archetype analysis and demographic research is choosing a scale of analysis. We selected the county as our unit of analysis because it was the smallest unit possible in Census of Agriculture data, which we needed to describe agricultural changes. However, our study area has counties of very different sizes, some of which are very large. Large counties may actually contain dynamics of multiple archetypes, which we are not able to capture when using the county as a base unit. For example, Owyhee County, the largest in our study area, was assigned the most rural archetypes where farmland is least threatened by development (R5-A5), yet our preliminary qualitative data shows that the most northern part of the county is experiencing the effects of urban sprawl from bordering Ada County [R1-A1, @daumale2026]. Qualitative social science is critical for both validating the usefulness of archetypes and revealing important nuance in larger geographical areas.

# Conclusions

## Farmlands are threatened by more than urban growth

R1, the cluster losing the most cropland and land in farms and gaining the most developed land, contains both counties that exhibit the traditional patterns of urban sprawl (i.e. Ada and Canyon counties). However, other archetypes are also losing land in farms and gaining developed land (R2, R3), just at lower rates. Future research should study if these archetypes exhibit any spatial patterns of development that can be used to inform future spatial land use change models, since standard urban growth models are likely a poor fit and would not generate realistic predictions. For example, the Farms Under Theat models have underpredicted farmland loss in Idaho.

## Building block archetypes for the resources and actors of a county as well as its history give us the fuller picture

I'd like to argue that resource archetypes indicate risk of certain causes/phenomena of farmland loss (i.e. urban sprawl, amenity migration, industrialization), and actor archetypes are how we see those phenomena play out. For example, Ada County has both the "risk of urban sprawl" archetype (R1) and the actor archetype that indicates urban sprawl is occurring (A1). On the other hand, Canyon always has the "risk of urban sprawl" archetype (R1) but transitioned to A1 in 2010, indicating the process of urban sprawl spread there between 2000 and 2010. 

Dynamic archetype analysis (finding archetypes through time) is an especially useful tool for considering multifaceted SES dynamics through time. Longitudinally comparable datasets are important for this work, but in this analysis, we've laid the blueprint to use public data in this way for any region in the US.

## Archetype analysis links spatially disparate but thematically similar counties

This analysis recontextualizes counties in the study area, allowing us to link counties that are spatially distant but have similar resources and actors. For example, the R5 (rural ag as amenity) counties north of the TV and around Jerome are spatially distant but show the same dynamics of migration for the amenity of agriculture (cite relevant studies).

# Main Takeaways

## Farmlands are threatened by more than urban growth

The original inspiration for this dissertation chapter was the observation that farmland loss prediction models underestimate farmland loss that isn't associated with urban growth. This analysis, and especially archetype R1, show that the average condition for this study area is farmland loss in places without large urban areas.

## Archetype analysis links spatially disparate but thematically similar counties

This analysis recontextualizes counties in the study area, allowing us to link counties that are spatially distant but have similar resources and actors. For example, though Twin Falls is far from Jefferson, both experience similar types of land use change and have the similar types of actors, and thus may borrow successful farmland protection strategies from each other. 

## Resource systems did not transition, even when actors changed. However, A1 actors in particular can lead to within-cluster shifts

Overall, I found that resource archetypes remained stable over this 40 year period while actor archetypes were more likely to change. This is reasonable for two reasons: (1) populations are more mobile than land systems, so it is easier for them to change, and (2) the difference between land systems (e.g. the dry shrublands of Owyhee and the forested recreation lands of Blaine) is greater than the difference between human populations, so it would require a greater change to shift resource archetypes compared to actor archetypes.

The presence of A1 actors (educated, growing, urban population) is associated with changes in resource systems, even if no counties transitioned from one resource archetype to another. Counties with A1 actors tend to accelerate their developed land growth and housing density. However, A1 does not always mean accelerated development, as evidenced by Blaine County, which has had wealthy inhabitants for a long time and has implemented land protections so that their resource system more closely matches more isolated counties.

-->

# Appendix A: Data Sources, Processing, and Summary Statistics

## Data Sources and Processing

Code for data retrieval and processing can be found in [notebooks/data_retrieval.qmd](https://github.com/CarolynKoehn/FarmPrES-archetypes/blob/main/notebooks/data_retrieval.qmd). We used the `tidyverse` for data cleaning [v2.0.0, @tidyverse] and the `terra` [v1.7.71, @terra] and `sf` [v1.0.16, @sf] packages for raster and vector data processing, respectively.

Census of Agriculture data was published for 1992, 2002, 2012, and 2022, so data from these years was used to represent agricultural indicators in 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. All Census of Agriculture data was downloaded at the county scale.

For all indicators that were simplified to principal components with principal component analysis, we retained principal components that explained >70% of the variance according to @aho2022.

### Resources

#### Percent land in farms

Land in farms and total county land data for 2002-2022 are available in the Census of Agriculture and were retrieved with the USDA NASS API [@CofAg_quickstats] using R package `rnassqs` [v0.6.1, @rnassqs]. Data for 1992 were digitized from the Census of Agriculture Historical Archive, 1992, Idaho, Chapter 2, Table 6 [@CofAg_1992_landinfarms].

#### Percent cropland

Annual land cover data from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) was downloaded from https://www.mrlc.gov/viewer/ [@nlcd]. We used the `exactextractr` package to summarize the percent cover of each land cover category in each county [v0.10.0, @exactextractr]. To calculate percent cropland, we used the sum of the "Pasture/Hay" and "Cultivated Crops" categories.

#### Percent forestland

Annual land cover data from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) was downloaded from https://www.mrlc.gov/viewer/ [@nlcd]. We used the `exactextractr` package to summarize the percent cover of each land cover category in each county [v0.10.0, @exactextractr]. To calculate percent forestland, we used the sum of the "Deciduous Forest" and "Evergreen Forest" categories.

#### Percent shrubland

Annual land cover data from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) was downloaded from https://www.mrlc.gov/viewer/ [@nlcd]. We used the `exactextractr` package to summarize the percent cover of each land cover category in each county [v0.10.0, @exactextractr]. To calculate percent shrubland, we used the "Shrub/Scrub" category.

#### Percent federally managed land {#sec-fedlands}

We used the 2023 BLM Idaho Surface Management Agency (Surface Ownership) dataset to represent federal lands [@blm_sma]. We classified the following management agency codes as federal land: BLM, BOR, COE, DOE, DOI, FAA, FHA, GSA, LU_DOI, LU_USDA, MIL, NPS, NWR, USDA, USFS. We then calculated the percent area covered by these management agencies in each county. This indicator was time invariable; federal lands are assumed to not be sold or acquired over the 40 year time period.

#### Lake area

Lake area data is from the Hydrosheds HydroLAKES product [v1.0, @hydrolakes]. We calculated the total area in square kilometers of lakes larger than 10 ha in each county. This indicator is time invariable; we assumed that lake area would not change since 1990.

#### Miles of river

We accessed river data from the WWF HydroSHEDS Free Flowing Rivers Network [v1.0, @hydrosheds] in Google Earth Engine. We filtered to rivers of order 7 or lower which have long-term average discharge >0.1 cubic meters per second. Then, we found the total length of rivers in each county and divided by the county area, so that river length units are in $km/km^2$. This indicator is time invariable; we assumed that river length would not change since 1990.

#### Percent developed land

Annual land cover data from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) was downloaded from https://www.mrlc.gov/viewer/ [@nlcd]. We used the `exactextractr` package to summarize the percent cover of each land cover category in each county [v0.10.0, @exactextractr]. To calculate percent developed land, we used the sum of the "Developed, Open Space", "Developed, Low Intensity", "Developed, Medium Intensity", and "Developed High Intensity" categories.

#### Land in, nearby, and far from urban areas {#sec-urbareas}

Since the definition of urban area changed for the 2020 census, we recreate urban areas for 1990-2020 with the 2020 definitions and thresholds. We first downloaded population size and housing unit count data for census blocks, 1990-2020, within 150 miles of Idaho from IPUMS [@ipums]. Then, we designated any census blocks with housing density $\geq$425 $units/mi^2$ as initial urban core blocks. Then, we added adjacent census blocks with housing density $\geq$200 $units/mi^2$ to the urban cores, repeating this process until there were no census blocks with housing density $\geq$200 $units/mi^2$ adjacent to the urban cores. Finally, we filtered out any urban cores without a high density urban nucleus, defined as a census block with housing density $\geq$1,275 $units/mi^2$, and we filtered out any urban cores with $\leq$2,000 houses or $\leq$5,000 residents. After these urban areas were established, land in each county was classified as "within an urban area," "within 10 mi of an urban area," "within 20 mi of an urban area," increasing in units of 10 mi, with the final category being ">100 mi from an urban area." Then, we calculated the percent cover of each category in each county. This process was repeated for each year, as population growth shifted urban boundaries and created new urban areas. Then, these data were used in a principal component analysis. We retained the first two principal components, which explained 75.8% of the variance.

#### Farm density

Number of farms and total county land data for 2002-2022 are available in the Census of Agriculture and were retrieved with the USDA NASS API [@CofAg_quickstats] using R package `rnassqs` [v0.6.1, @rnassqs]. Data for 1992 were digitized from the Census of Agriculture Historical Archive, 1992, Idaho, Chapter 2, Table 6 [@CofAg_1992_landinfarms].

#### Percent land in recreation areas

We used data from the Protected Areas Database, which "was originally designed to support biodiversity assessments; however, its scope expanded in recent years to include all public and nonprofit held lands and waters" [@pad_us].

The following land designations (column `Des_Tp`) were considered recreation lands to calculate percent recreation land in this analysis: Recreation Management Area, National Monument, National Park, State Recreation Area, State Park, National Recreation Area, National Scenic or Historic Trail. Since sas some state parks were misclassified, these additional local designation (column `Loc_Ds`) terms related to recreation were added as well: State Park, Recreation Reservoir, National Recreation Trail, Recreation Area, National Recreation Area, National Monument, SREC, REC, SP, National Park, and Designated - Recreational. To capture time series data, we filtered data by date established and only included parks established before each time point 1990-2020. Parks without an establishment date were assumed to be established before 1990. We calculated the percent area covered by these recreation lands for each county and year.

#### Distance to nearest national park

We calculated the Euclidean distance from the edge of each county to the edge of the closest national park in the PAD-US data [@pad_us]. This indicator was time invariable, as all nearby national parks were established before 1990.

#### Distance to nearest ski area

We calculated the Euclidean distance from the edge of each county to the edge of the closest ski area in the PAD-US data [@pad_us]. This indicator was time invariable, as all nearby ski resorts were in use before 1990.

#### Housing density

Data for the number of houses in each county for 2000-2020 was downloaded via the Census API [@decennial_2000; @decennial_2010; @decennial_2020] using the `tidycensus` package [v1.6.3, @tidycensus]. Data for 1990 were digitized from the 1990 Census of Population and Housing [1990 CPH-2-14, @CofPopHous_1990]. We used total county land from the Census of Agriculture retrieved for 2002-2022 from the USDA NASS API [@CofAg_quickstats] using R package `rnassqs` [v0.6.1, @rnassqs] and digitized for 1992 from the Census of Agriculture Historical Archive, 1992, Idaho, Chapter 2, Table 6 [@CofAg_1992_landinfarms].

#### Non-federal land near major roadway

First, we downloaded primary and secondary road shapefiles from the US Census TIGER/Line shapefiles [@tiger_line] using the`tigris` package [v2.1, @tigris]. Primary roads "are generally divided limited-access highways within the Federal interstate highway system or under state management," and secondary roads are "main arteries, usually in the U.S. highway, state highway, or county highway system" [@tiger_line_docs]. Then, we created a 10km buffer around the road shapefiles, cropping out federal lands described in @sec-fedlands. We then calculated the percent of the county covered by non-federal lands within 10 km of a primary or secondary road.

#### Healthcare workers per 1000 residents

We downloaded data for public sector health workers from the Census of Governments [@aspep1997; @aspep2002; @aspep2012; @aspep2022]. We added local government employees in the "Health" and "Hospitals" categories. Because the first available dataset from the Census of Governments is from 1997, and subsequent Census of Governments data collection happens in years ending with -2, we used 1997 employment data for 1990, 2002 employment data for 2000, 2012 employment data for 2010, and 2022 employment data for 2020.

We downloaded data for private sector health workers from the County Business Patterns series from the U.S. Census Bureau [@cbp1997; @cbp2002; @cbp2012; @cbp2022] using the `censusapi` package [v0.9.0, @censusapi]. We used comparable SIC and NAICS codes to sum the total healthcare workers in each county for each year:

- 1997: SIC codes 8010 (Offices and clinics of medical doctors), 8060 (Hospitals), and 8080	(Home health care services)
- 2002-2022: NAICS codes 621111 (Offices of physicians exc mental health), 622 (Hospitals), and 621610 (Home health care services)

Population counts for each county for 2000-2020 were downloaded via the Census API [@decennial_2000; @decennial_2010; @decennial_2020] using the `tidycensus` package [v1.6.3, @tidycensus]. Data for 1990 were downloaded from the National Bureau of Economic Research [@cencounts]. We divided the total number of healthcare workers by the total population count in each county and decade.

#### Average slope

We downloaded elevation data from Terrain Tiles [@aws_terrain] via the `elevatr` package [v0.99.0, @elevatr] at a resolution of 106.8872 meters. We calculated the slope from the elevation data and averaged the slope values within each county. This indicator is time invariant; we assume that the average slope will not change through time.

#### Percent change in number of farms

Number of farms data for 1997-2022 are available in the Census of Agriculture and were retrieved with the USDA NASS API [@CofAg_quickstats] using R package `rnassqs` [v0.6.1, @rnassqs]. Data for 1987-1992 were digitized from the Census of Agriculture Historical Archive, 1992, Idaho, Chapter 2, Table 6 [@CofAg_1992_landinfarms].

We calculated the five-year percent change in number of farms before each time point. For example, for 2022: $(Farms_{2022} - Farms_{2017}) / Farms_{2017}$

#### Percent change of land in farms

Land in farms data for 1997-2022 are available in the Census of Agriculture and were retrieved with the USDA NASS API [@CofAg_quickstats] using R package `rnassqs` [v0.6.1, @rnassqs]. Data for 1987-1992 were digitized from the Census of Agriculture Historical Archive, 1992, Idaho, Chapter 2, Table 6 [@CofAg_1992_landinfarms]. We used the five-year change in the percent of all county land that was in farms.

#### Percent change of cropland

Annual land cover data from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) was downloaded from https://www.mrlc.gov/viewer/ [@nlcd]. We used the `exactextractr` package to summarize the percent cover of each land cover category in each county [v0.10.0, @exactextractr]. To calculate percent cropland, we used the sum of the "Pasture/Hay" and "Cultivated Crops" categories. We used the five-year change in the percent of all county land that was in cropland.

#### Percent change of forest

Annual land cover data from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) was downloaded from https://www.mrlc.gov/viewer/ [@nlcd]. We used the `exactextractr` package to summarize the percent cover of each land cover category in each county [v0.10.0, @exactextractr]. To calculate percent cropland, we used the sum of the "Deciduous Forest" and "Evergreen Forest" categories. We used the five-year change in the percent of all county land that was in forestland.

#### Percent change of shrubland

Annual land cover data from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) was downloaded from https://www.mrlc.gov/viewer/ [@nlcd]. We used the `exactextractr` package to summarize the percent cover of each land cover category in each county [v0.10.0, @exactextractr]. To calculate percent cropland, we used the "Shrub/Scrub category. We used the five-year change in the percent of all county land that was in shrubland.

#### Percent change of developed land

Annual land cover data from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) was downloaded from https://www.mrlc.gov/viewer/ [@nlcd]. We used the `exactextractr` package to summarize the percent cover of each land cover category in each county [v0.10.0, @exactextractr]. To calculate percent cropland, we used the sum of the "Developed, Open Space", "Developed, Low Intensity", "Developed, Medium Intensity", and "Developed High Intensity" categories. We used the five-year change in the percent of all county land that was in developed land.

#### Percent farms with net loss

Farms with net loss and total farms data for 2002-2022 are available in the Census of Agriculture and were retrieved with the USDA NASS API [@CofAg_quickstats] using R package `rnassqs` [v0.6.1, @rnassqs]. Data for 1992 were digitized from the Census of Agriculture Historical Archive, 1992, Idaho, Chapter 2, Table 4 [@CofAg_1992_netloss].

#### Agriculture support jobs

We downloaded data from the County Business Patterns series [@cbp1997; @cbp2002; @cbp2012; @cbp2022] using the `censusapi` package [v0.9.0, @censusapi]. We used comparable SIC and NAICS codes to sum the total agriculture support workers in each county for each year:

- 1990: SIC codes 0710 (Soil Preparation Services), 0720 (Crop Services), 0761 (Farm Labor and Management Services), 0750 (Animal Services except veterinary)
- 2000-2020: NAICS codes 115112 (Soil Preparation, Planting, and Cultivating), 115113 (Crop Harvesting Primarily by Machine), 115114 (Postharvest Crop Activities), 115115 (Farm Labor Contractors and Crew Leaders), 115116 (Farm Management Services), 115210 (Support Activities for Animal Production)

We also downloaded the number of hired workers from the Census of Agriculture for 2002-2022 using the the USDA NASS API [@CofAg_quickstats] with R package `rnassqs` [v0.6.1, @rnassqs]. Data for 1992 were digitized from the Census of Agriculture Historical Archive, 1992, Idaho, Chapter 2, Table 5 [@CofAg_1992_hiredlabor].

Population counts for each county for 2000-2020 were downloaded via the Census API [@decennial_2000; @decennial_2010; @decennial_2020] using the `tidycensus` package [v1.6.3, @tidycensus]. Data for 1990 were downloaded from the National Bureau of Economic Research [@cencounts]. We divided the total number of agriculture support workers by the total population count in each county and year.

#### Hotel and restaurant jobs

We downloaded data from the County Business Patterns series [@cbp1997; @cbp2002; @cbp2012; @cbp2022] using the `censusapi` package [v0.9.0, @censusapi]. We used comparable SIC and NAICS codes to sum the total hospitality workers in each county for each year:

- 1990: SIC codes 7000 (Hotels and Other Lodging Places), 5800 (Eating and drinking places)
- 2000-2020: NAICS code 72 (Accommodation and food services)

Population counts for each county for 2000-2020 were downloaded via the Census API [@decennial_2000; @decennial_2010; @decennial_2020] using the `tidycensus` package [v1.6.3, @tidycensus]. Data for 1990 were downloaded from the National Bureau of Economic Research [@cencounts]. We divided the total number of hospitality workers by the total population count in each county and year.

#### Median home value

Data for the median home value in each county for 2000-2020 were downloaded via the Census API [@decennial_2000; @acs2010; @acs2020] using the `tidycensus` package [v1.6.3, @tidycensus]. Data for 1990 were digitized from the 1990 Census of Housing [1990 CH-1-14, @CofHous_1990]. We adjusted for inflation by converting all dollar amounts to 2020 US dollars using the consumer price indices for housing in December of each year [@cpiu_housing].

#### Farm size

Number of farms in each size class and total farms data for 2002-2022 are available in the Census of Agriculture and were retrieved with the USDA NASS API [@CofAg_quickstats] using R package `rnassqs` [v0.6.1, @rnassqs]. Data for 1992 were digitized from the Census of Agriculture Historical Archive, 1992, Idaho, Chapter 2, Table 6 [@CofAg_1992_landinfarms]. We found the percent of farms in each size category available for each year, and then simplified the data using principal component analysis. We retained the first two principal components, which explained 81.1% of the variance.

### Actors

#### Population density

Population counts for each county for 2000-2020 were downloaded via the Census API [@decennial_2000; @decennial_2010; @decennial_2020] using the `tidycensus` package [v1.6.3, @tidycensus]. Data for 1990 were downloaded from the National Bureau of Economic Research [@cencounts]. We divided by total county land from the Census of Agriculture retrieved for 2002-2022 from the USDA NASS API [@CofAg_quickstats] using R package `rnassqs` [v0.6.1, @rnassqs] and digitized for 1992 from the Census of Agriculture Historical Archive, 1992, Idaho, Chapter 2, Table 6 [@CofAg_1992_landinfarms].

#### Population change

Population counts for each county for 2000-2020 were downloaded via the Census API [@decennial_2000; @decennial_2010; @decennial_2020] using the `tidycensus` package [v1.6.3, @tidycensus]. Data for 1980-1990 were downloaded from the National Bureau of Economic Research [@cencounts]. We used the percent different of population over a 10 year period; for example: $ (population_{1990} - population_{1980}) / population_{1980} $.

#### Percent employed in different industries

Because the first available dataset from the Census of Governments, which provides a full dataset of employees in the public sector, is from 1997, and subsequent Census of Governments data collection happens in years ending with -2, we used 1997 data for 1990, 2002 data for 2000, 2012 data for 2010, and 2022 data for 2020.

We downloaded data for private sector jobs from the County Business Patterns series [@cbp1997; @cbp2002; @cbp2012; @cbp2022] using the `censusapi` package [v0.9.0, @censusapi]. We summed jobs in the following categories based on which high-level SIC and NAICS codes were comparable:

- Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Hunting: SIC code 7 (Agricultural Services, Forestry, and Fishing), NAICS code 11 (Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Hunting)
- Mining, Quarrying, and Oil and Gas Extraction: SIC code 10 (Mining), NAICS code 21 (Mining, Quarrying, and Oil and Gas Extraction)
- Construction: SIC code 15 (Construction), NAICS code 23 (Construction)
- Manufacturing: SIC code 20 (Manufacturing), NAICS code "31-33" (Manufacturing)
- Trucking and warehousing: SIC code 4200 (Trucking and warehousing), NAICS codes 484 (Truck Transportation) and 493 (Warehousing and Storage)
- Wholesale Trade: SIC code 50 (Wholesale Trade), NAICS code 42 (Wholesale Trade)
- Retail Trade: SIC code 52 (Retail Trade), NAICS code "44-45" (Retail Trade)
- Finance, Insurance, and Real Estate: SIC code 60 (Finance, Insurance, and Real Estate), NAICS codes 52 (Finance and Insurance) and 531 (Real Estate)
- Legal: SIC code 8100 (Legal services), NAICS code 5411 (Legal Services)
- Education and libraries: SIC code 8200 (Educational services), NAICS codes 61 (Educational Services) and 519120 (Libraries and Archives)
- Health and social services: SIC codes 8000 (Health services) and 8300 (Social services), NAICS code 62 (Health Care and Social Assistance)
- Accommodation and Food: SIC codes 7000 (Hotels and Other Lodging Places) and 5800 (Eating and drinking places), NAICS code 72 (Accommodation and Food Services)
- Recreation: SIC code 7900 (Amusement and recreation services), NAICS codes 71 (Arts, Entertainment, and Recreation) and 611620 (Sports and Recreation Instruction)

The County Business Patterns data does not include public sector employees or agricultural producers. We used data from the Annual Survey of Public Employment & Payroll [@aspep1997; @aspep2002; @aspep2012; @aspep2022] to add public employees to the following categories:

- Legal: ASPEP government function category "Judicial & Legal"
- Education and libraries: ASPEP government function categories "Libraries", "Education - Elementary and Secondary Instructional", and "Education - Elementary and Secondary Other"
- Health and social services: ASPEP government function categories "Health", "Hospitals", "Housing & Community Development", and "Public Welfare"
- Recreation: ASPEP government function category "Parks & Recreation"

We used data from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages [@qcew] to quantify employees of the state or federal government residing in each county. Finally, we added producer counts from the Census of Agriculture using the USDA NASS API [@CofAg_quickstats] with R package `rnassqs` [v0.6.1, @rnassqs] for 1997-2022 since the County Business Patterns data did not include agricultural production.

We calculated the percent of workers in each category, then used these data in a principal component analysis. We retained the first three components, which explained 73.1% of the variance.

#### Percent retired

We defined retirees as residents over age 65 who were not in the labor force. Population counts and counts of people >65 not in the labor force for each county for 2000-2020 were downloaded via the Census API [@decennial_2000; @acs2010; @acs2020] using the `tidycensus` package [v1.6.3, @tidycensus]. Labor force data for 1990 were digitized from Table 144 of the 1990 Census of Population for Idaho [1990 CP-2-14, @CofPop_1990]. Population count data for 1990 were downloaded from the National Bureau of Economic Research [@cencounts].

#### Average age

Data on the weighted average age of residents in each county from 1969-2023 were downloaded from the @nih_age. 

#### Median household income

Data for the median household income in each county for 2000-2020 was downloaded via the Census API [@decennial_2000; @acs2010; @acs2020] using the `tidycensus` package [v1.6.3, @tidycensus]. Data for 1990 were digitized from from Table 148 of the 1990 Census of Population for Idaho [1990 CP-2-14, @CofHous_1990]. We adjusted for inflation by converting all dollar amounts to 2020 US dollars using the consumer price indices for all items in the Western United States (series ID CUUR0400SA0) in December of each year [@cpiu_all].

#### Unemployment rate

We downloaded monthly unemployment rate data from @unemployment and used the mean unemployment rate across months for each county and year.

#### Education level -- high school or Bachelor's degree

We downloaded data on the percentage of residents whose highest level of education was high school or a Bachelor's degree from @education. We used the column "2008-2012" to represent 2010 and the column "2019-2023" to represent 2020.

#### Racial composition

Population counts for each race used by the US Census for each county for 2000-2020 were downloaded via the Census API [@decennial_2000; @decennial_2010; @decennial_2020_dhc] using the `tidycensus` package [v1.6.3, @tidycensus]. Data for 1990 were digitized from Table 6 of the 1990 Census of Population for Idaho [1990 CP-2-14, @CofPop_1990]. We simplified these data with principle component analysis, retaining the first component which explained 95.3% of the variance.

#### Hispanic ethnicity

Population counts and ethnicity data for each county for 2000-2020 were downloaded via the Census API [@decennial_2000; @decennial_2010; @decennial_2020_dhc] using the `tidycensus` package [v1.6.3, @tidycensus]. Data for 1990 were digitized from Table 6 of the 1990 Census of Population for Idaho [1990 CP-2-14, @CofPop_1990].

#### Farm tenure

Number of farms in each tenure class (full-owned, part-owned, and tenant) and total farms data for 2002-2022 are available in the Census of Agriculture and were retrieved with the USDA NASS API [@CofAg_quickstats] using R package `rnassqs` [v0.6.1, @rnassqs]. Data for 1992 were digitized from the Census of Agriculture Historical Archive, 1992, Idaho, Chapter 2, Table 11 [@CofAg_1992_tenure]. We found the percent of farms in each tenure category for each year, and then simplified the data using principal component analysis. We retained the first principal component, which explained 92.6% of the variance.

#### Number of hired agricultural workers

We downloaded the number of hired workers from the Census of Agriculture for 2002-2022 using the the USDA NASS API [@CofAg_quickstats] with R package `rnassqs` [v0.6.1, @rnassqs]. Data for 1992 were digitized from the Census of Agriculture Historical Archive, 1992, Idaho, Chapter 2, Table 5 [@CofAg_1992_hiredlabor].

#### Geographical isolation

We calculated a custom county-level proxy for the Rural-Urban Commuting Area [RUCA] codes [@ruca] that could be compared across time. We first used the urban areas we computed (methods in @sec-urbareas) to designate counties as metropolitan (contain an urban area with population >50,000), micropolitan (largest urban area has population 10,000-49,999), small town (largest urban area has population <9,999), or rural (no urban area). Then, we used county-to-county commuting flow data [@commute1990; @commute2000; @commute2010; @commute2020] to calculate how many workers from each county commuted to six types of counties: metropolitan, micropolitan, small town, rural, >150 mile commute, or work and live in the same county. We also created two categories for residents of a metropolitan county who commuted to a county with a larger or smaller metropolitan area (by population size). In total, we had 25 commuting categories, which we simplified through principal component analysis. We retained the first two components, which explained 80.3% of the variance.

## Summary Statistics

### Resources

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: "R data"

r1 <- clust_dat[["Resource"]]

r1_means <- r1 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            median = median(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(var_name_clean = factor(input_data_name,
                                 levels = c("land_in_farms", "percent_cropland", "percent_forest", "percent_shrubland", "perc_fed", "lake_area_km2", "rivers_km_per_km2", "urb_dist_pc1", "urb_dist_pc2", "percent_developed", "farms_per_acre", "perc_rec", "dist_to_ski", "dist_to_NP", "housing_units_per_acre", "perc_non_fed_road_area_km2", "healthworkers_per_1000", "perc_farms_change", "Perc_change_land_in_farms", "cropland_change", "forest_change", "shrub_change", "developed_change", "perc_farms_w_net_loss", "ag_support_per_1000", "accom_food_per_1000", "med_home_val_in_2020_USD", "farm_size_pc1", "farm_size_pc2", "avg_slope"),
                                 labels = c("Land in Farms", "Cropland", "Forest", "Shrubland", "Federal Land", "Lake Area", "Length of Rivers", "Distance from Urban (PC1)", "Distance from Urban (PC2)","Developed Land", "Farm Density", "Recreation Land", "Distance to a Ski Area", "Distance to a National Park", "Housing Density", "Non-Federal Land near Highway", "Healthcare Workers", "Farm Loss/Gain", "Land in Farms Loss/Gain", "Cropland Loss/Gain", "Forest Loss/Gain", "Shrubland Loss/Gain", "Developed Land Gain", "Farms with Net Loss", "Jobs Supporting Ag", "Jobs in Hospitality", "Med Home Value", "Farm Size (PC1)", "Farm Size (PC2)", "Average Slope"))) %>%
  arrange(var_name_clean) %>%
  relocate(var_name_clean, .before = input_data_name) %>%
  select(-input_data_name)

# write.csv(farm_sizes,
#           "../data/API_data_download_backup/farm_sizes.csv",
#           row.names = FALSE)

# clean
farm_sizes2 <- farm_sizes %>%
  # remove redundant categories
  filter(!(domaincat_desc %in% c("AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 219 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (220 TO 259 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (260 TO 499 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (50.0 TO 69.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (70.0 TO 99.9 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (100 TO 139 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (140 TO 179 ACRES)",
                                 "AREA OPERATED: (1,000 OR MORE ACRES)"))) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(county_name, year),
              names_from = domaincat_desc,
              values_from = Value) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(total_farms = sum(c_across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`), na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(across(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`:`AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`,
                ~.x/total_farms*100),
         year = as.integer(year))

# 1992 data
farm_sizes_1992 <- read.csv("data/Farm_size_1925-1992.csv") %>%
  filter(Year == 1992) %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c("County", "Year"),
              names_from = "Size",
              values_from = "Num_farms") %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(across(`under 10 acres`:`over 2,000 acres`,
                ~.x/`all farms`*100)) %>%
  # create comparable categories
  mutate(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)` = `1,000 to 1,999 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)` = `under 10 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)` = `10 to 49 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)` = `180 to 219 acres` + `220 to 259 acres` + `260 to 499 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)` = `over 2,000 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)` = `50 to 69 acres` + `70 to 99 acres` + `100 to 139 acres` + `140 to 179 acres`,
         `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)` = `500 to 999 acres`) %>%
  rename("county_name" = "County",
         "year" = "Year")

# join
farm_sizes_all <- rbind(farm_sizes2[,1:9],
                        farm_sizes_1992[,c(1:2,16:22)]) %>%
  replace(is.na(.), 0) %>%
  mutate(county = str_to_title(county_name),
         year = as.integer(year)-2)

farm_sizes_r1 <- left_join(r1, farm_sizes_all, by = c("county", "year")) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(small_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1.0 TO 9.9 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (10.0 TO 49.9 ACRES)`),
         med_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (50 TO 179 ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (180 TO 499 ACRES)`),
         large_farm_perc = sum(`AREA OPERATED: (1,000 TO 1,999 ACRES)`,
                               `AREA OPERATED: (2,000 OR MORE ACRES)`,
                             `AREA OPERATED: (500 TO 999 ACRES)`))

###############
# urb areas
urb_dist_areas_r1 <- read.csv("data/clean_data_for_PCA/urb_dist_areas.csv") %>%
  pivot_longer(!c("county", "year"),
               names_to = "dist",
               values_to = "perc") %>%
  mutate(dist = as.integer(str_extract_all(dist, "\\d+"))) %>%
  mutate(label = ifelse(dist == 0, "Urban",
                        ifelse(dist <= 50, "Within 50", "Over 50"))) %>%
  group_by(county, year, label) %>%
  summarise(urb_cat_perc = sum(perc))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
#| label: "A data"

a1 <- clust_dat[["Actors"]]

a1_means <- a1 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  pivot_longer(!c(county, year, cluster, GEOID),
               names_to = "input_data_name",
               values_to = "input_data_value") %>%
  group_by(input_data_name) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            median = median(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            min = min(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE),
            max = max(input_data_value, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(var_name_clean = factor(input_data_name,
                                 levels = c("pop_per_acre", "perc_pop_change", "emply_pc1", "emply_pc2", "emply_pc3", "perc_retired", "avg_age", "med_income_in_2020_USD", "unemployment_rate", "High.school", "Bachelors", "races_PC1", "perc_hispanic", "tenure_pc1", "perc_farms_w_net_loss", "num_hired", "ruca_proxy_pc1", "ruca_proxy_pc2"),
                                 labels = c("Population Density", "Population Change", "Employment Sectors (PC1)", "Employment Sectors (PC2)", "Employment Sectors (PC3)", "Retirees", "Average Age", "Median Income", "Unemployment Rate", "Residents with High School Education", "Residents with Bachelor's", "Racial Composition (PC1)", "Hispanic Residents", "Full Owned Farms", "Farms with Net Loss", "Hired Ag Workers", "Geographical Isolation (PC1)", "Geographical Isolation (PC2)"))) %>%
  arrange(var_name_clean) %>%
  relocate(var_name_clean, .before = input_data_name) %>%
  select(-input_data_name)
```

Summary statistics for all study area counties. A selection of geographical isolation statistics are reported (all commute types used by >10% of a county's workforce) as there were very many (25) commute type possibilities in the study area, and means are not reported as they were not representative of the overall data spread.
